title: Swap per-GPU weight copies for an optical weight-broadcast tree
idea: Substitute storage with broadcast. Instead of every accelerator keeping its own copy of the model weights in HBM, a central weight store streams each layer's weights over a WDM optical broadcast tree, timed to the synchronized decode step, so each of N accelerators buffers only the 1-2 layers in flight in SRAM. HBM is left for KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are copied 8-64x across a serving pod. One copy plus broadcast (~1.4 TB/s for a 70B fp8 model at 20 steps/s) cuts weight-resident HBM ~Nx, freeing 50-90% of HBM in weight-dominated serving. Attacks the HBM TSV tax and capital intensity.

title: Swap DRAM KV cache for an append-only log on write-once NVM
idea: Substitute DRAM with endurance-limited NVM by matching the workload: KV entries are written once and read thousands of times, so an HBM-style stack of dense PCM/RRAM dies holds them as an append-only log. The accelerator prefetches the next layer's KV into SRAM while the current layer computes, which hides the ~100-300 ns NVM reads. A conversation's whole region is erased at once when it ends, so each cell sees only ~1e5-1e6 writes in its lifetime.
why: KV cache is 30-70% of HBM demand in long-context serving. The write-once pattern sidesteps NVM's endurance limit, so 2-3x fewer DRAM bits are needed per served token.

title: Swap HBM-resident KV for attention-computing commodity DDR PIM DIMMs
idea: Substitute expensive HBM bits with cheap DDR bits. The KV cache moves to DDR5 DIMMs whose buffer chips hold bank-group dot-product and softmax units; the GPU sends only the query vector and gets back the attention output, so KV bytes never cross the bus.
why: HBM uses ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6). Moving KV, often more than half of HBM demand, to DDR PIM halves HBM per accelerator, needs ~3x less wafer per KV bit, and cuts data-movement pJ (fact 5).

title: Swap word-granularity tiering for bit-plane significance tiering
idea: Substitute the word with the bit-plane as the unit of placement. Tensors are stored transposed into bit-planes: the memory controller keeps the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes in DRAM and the low-order planes in CXL flash. Kernels compute first on the coarse planes and fetch low planes only for rows where an error-bound or confidence check fails.
why: Most ML reads need only 4-6 of 16 bits. Full values stay recoverable while DRAM-resident bits drop 2-3x for weights and activations, which improves cost per bit and energy per useful bit.

title: Swap SSD DRAM mapping tables for learned piecewise-linear FTL in SRAM
idea: Substitute the SSD's DRAM logical-to-physical map (~1 GB per TB) with a learned index of piecewise-linear segments held in controller SRAM. The FTL lays out writes in a log-structured way to keep segments long, and a small exact table catches outliers.
why: Enterprise SSDs use a noticeable share of DRAM bit shipments (exabytes of flash at 1 GB/TB). A 50-200x smaller map removes nearly all SSD DRAM and returns that supply to servers.

title: Swap HBM weight storage for read-only stacked NAND beside smaller HBM
idea: Substitute HBM with high-bandwidth stacked NAND for the read-only tier. Inference weights do not change for months, so a wide, many-plane NAND die stack on the same interposer streams them into SRAM in 4-16 KB pages, and HBM shrinks to KV cache and activations. Endurance does not matter because weights are written only at model deployment.
why: Weights are 40-70% of accelerator memory. NAND is ~10x cheaper per bit and needs no EUV for capacity, so HBM per accelerator falls ~2x, and the HBM TSV tax falls with it.

title: Swap stored weight matrices for an on-chip PRNG weight synthesizer
idea: Substitute stored bits with regenerated bits. Each weight block is post-fit as a few coefficients times matrices from a seeded LFSR basis, and a hardware synthesizer next to the tensor cores regenerates the block in SRAM from (seed, coefficients) at use time. DRAM holds only seeds and coefficients.
why: Trades cheap logic for scarce DRAM. About 3-4 bits per weight equivalent cuts weight DRAM 4-5x versus bf16 and cuts transfer energy (fact 5).

title: Swap per-host duplicate pages for one fleet-shared CXL read-only copy
idea: Substitute per-host duplicates with one rack copy. Read-only pages (kernel text, shared libraries, container layers, model weights, JIT code caches) are hashed across the rack, one canonical copy is stored in a CXL-switched memory appliance and mapped read-only into every host, and writes copy-on-write into local DRAM.
why: Same-host dedup (KSM) misses cross-host duplication. Rack-wide single copies recover an estimated 5-15% of fleet DRAM.

title: Swap fixed DIMM ownership for optically re-patched memory blades
idea: Substitute static wiring with a reconfigurable optical patch panel. Memory blades connect to servers through optical circuit switches, which reassign blades to servers every few minutes or hours following scheduler forecasts, so capacity physically follows demand.
why: Clouds strand ~25-35% of DRAM because each server is sized for its own peak. Moving capacity between servers cuts installed DRAM ~20% at equal service.

title: Swap local phone LPDDR for pooled edge DRAM for background apps
idea: Substitute on-device RAM with a shared edge pool. Phones freeze background apps and stream their compressed process images to edge-cloud DRAM over 5G and Wi-Fi, then restore them lazily through page-fault streaming. Statistical multiplexing lets one edge GB serve many phones.
why: Phones are roughly a third of DRAM bits and carry 8-16 GB mainly to keep apps warm. Phones could ship with 30-50% less LPDDR, with a much smaller pooled amount at the edge.

title: Swap raw bf16 in HBM for ANS-coded tensors decoded at load
idea: Substitute raw storage with entropy-coded storage. An asymmetric-numeral-system decoder in the GPU's L2-to-SM path, driven by a per-tile offset table, lets weights and KV live entropy-coded in HBM and expand transparently on load. bf16 exponents carry only ~2.6 bits of entropy, and activation tiles are often sparse.
why: A lossless 1.3-1.6x capacity gain on weights, more on sparse tensors, plus fewer pJ per useful bit moved (fact 5).

title: Swap 64-bit pointers for region-relative 32-bit pointer instructions
idea: Substitute absolute 64-bit pointers with hardware base-plus-offset addressing. New load and store instructions take a 32-bit offset from a per-region base register with a hardware bounds check, so C/C++ compilers can emit 32-bit pointers in heaps above 4 GB without software decode overhead.
why: Pointer-dense heaps (graphs, trees, object stores, databases) shrink 25-40%. Compressed oops already proves this in software, and the hardware path brings it to native code.

title: Swap separate host and device copies for one unified package memory
idea: Substitute the host-DRAM plus device-HBM pair with one coherent physical pool on a CPU+accelerator package. Data loader buffers, pinned staging areas and checkpoints then exist once instead of twice.
why: An 8-GPU AI node carries 1-2 TB of host DRAM, much of it staging copies. Unifying cuts DRAM per node 20-40%.

title: Swap all-DRAM main memory for a DRAM cache over SLC NAND
idea: Substitute most DRAM capacity with low-latency SLC NAND on a CXL device. A hardware-managed DRAM cache of about 1/8 of capacity sits in front, with page-level hot/cold tracking and a sector write-back buffer to protect endurance.
why: Most server memory is cold at any instant, so DRAM per server falls 4-8x for in-memory databases, caches and VM hosts, replaced by non-EUV NAND bits.

title: Swap DRAM-resident frozen weights for via-programmed 3D ROM chiplets
idea: Substitute rewritable DRAM with mask-programmed vertical ROM strings, NAND-like stacks whose bits are set by via or implant and never written, for open-weight models that stay frozen for a year. The chiplets are built on a mature U.S. line and swapped like cartridges when the model is upgraded.
why: No capacitor, no refresh and no EUV, made on domestic mature-node capital. Frees HBM for KV cache. The main risk is the model becoming obsolete, not physics.

title: Swap replicated cluster datasets for threads that migrate to data
idea: Substitute moving data with moving computation. On a remote access, a thread's ~200-byte context hops to the node that owns the data instead of the data being fetched or cached locally, so graph and sparse datasets are stored exactly once across the cluster.
why: Distributed graph analytics keeps 2-5x ghost and replica copies. Single-copy storage cuts cluster DRAM 2-3x for those workloads.

title: Swap per-token old KV for a holographic superposition trace
idea: Substitute discrete per-token storage with superposition. Each distant token's key and value are bound by circular convolution (holographic reduced representations) and added into a fixed d-dimensional trace per head. Recent tokens stay exact, queries unbind the trace for approximate recall, and the model is fine-tuned to tolerate the noise.
why: Old-context memory drops from O(n*d) to O(d) per head, 100x or more at 1M tokens, which caps the KV size for very long contexts. Quality is the risk.

title: Swap idle consumer RAM into a paid cold-cache donation network
idea: Substitute data-center cache DRAM with idle installed RAM. A client app rents a revocable, encrypted, erasure-coded slice of idle PC and console RAM to a CDN-style tier for cold, latency-tolerant objects, and pays owners in credits.
why: Raises usable supply without fabs: 1 GB on each of 50M devices is 50 PB of cache, which offloads warm-cache tiers in data centers.

title: Swap server-side user state for client-carried signed state blobs
idea: Substitute server memory with the client's memory. Recommendation and session services stop keeping per-user embeddings, histories and sessions in DRAM: each client holds its own encrypted, signed state vector of a few KB and attaches it to every request, and servers keep only shared item tables.
why: Per-user tables reach terabytes per model on large platforms, and moving them to clients removes a large share of recommendation-serving DRAM.

title: Swap new DIMMs for retired DDR4 behind CXL expanders
idea: Substitute new wafers with recycled bits. DDR4 harvested from decommissioned servers is tested, binned and mounted on CXL expanders as a second memory tier in new DDR5 servers, and OS tiering places cold pages on it.
why: Hundreds of PB of DDR4 retire each year. Recycled DDR4 can supply 20-30% of new-server capacity at a fraction of the new-DIMM cost, with zero new wafers.

title: Swap long agent context for sleep-phase consolidation into LoRA weights
idea: Substitute context with weights, the way the hippocampus hands memories to the cortex. A long-running agent periodically 'sleeps', distills its accumulated KV context into a small LoRA delta by test-time training, and then drops the KV.
why: A multi-day agent's KV grows to tens of GB. A 10-50 MB LoRA uses 100-1000x less memory, at the cost of extra compute and some recall error.

title: Swap fixed model size for nested sub-models that shrink with memory
idea: Substitute a fixed footprint with an elastic one. Matryoshka-style transformers are trained so that narrower sub-models are prefixes of the full weight matrices (the first k heads and MLP columns); when memory is scarce the server unmaps the tail columns and serves the nested model, then re-expands when memory frees up.
why: Memory becomes a dial, not a hard requirement: 2-4x less resident weight memory at peak scarcity, so fleets can be provisioned for average rather than peak load.

title: Swap small tokenizers for vocabulary transplants that shrink KV per text
idea: Substitute a 32k-token vocabulary with a 200k+ one tuned to code and multilingual text: new embeddings are initialized from compositions of old-token embeddings, then a short fine-tune follows. The same document becomes fewer tokens, so fewer KV entries.
why: KV memory scales with token count; 25-40% fewer tokens for code and non-English text cuts the KV cache proportionally on every request.

title: Swap scrapped retention-fail dies for an error-tolerant DRAM grade
idea: Substitute 'scrap' with 'approximate grade'. Dies that fail retention or margin screens are packaged as standard DDR5/LPDDR5 parts rated for a measured bit-error rate, and the OS and ML frameworks place only error-tolerant data on them (activations, media buffers, refetchable caches). DDR/HBM interfaces are unchanged.
why: Adds sellable bits with no new wafers by recovering several percent of test fallout, and loosens the leakage-tail screen (fact 3).

title: Swap discarded bad-row DIMMs for map-carrying discount DIMMs
idea: Substitute 'reject' with 'map and avoid'. Modules with failed rows or banks beyond post-package-repair capacity ship with a bad-address map in the SPD vendor area; firmware hands it to the OS, which never allocates those pages (as badram/memmap already allow). JEDEC signaling is untouched.
why: Raises module yield by a few percent at a discount price tier, adding usable supply through today's interface.

title: Swap ECC-chip overhead for end-to-end checksums on reloadable data
idea: Substitute hardware ECC with software integrity for data that can be reloaded. Model weights, container images and page-cache copies of files sit on non-ECC DIMMs, guarded by per-block hashes that a background scrubber checks; a mismatched block is simply re-read from SSD. ECC DIMMs keep only mutable state.
why: DDR5 ECC RDIMMs spend 20% of their chips (8 of 40 bits per subchannel) on ECC, and this reclaims those bits for the reloadable data class. Standard DIMMs and interfaces throughout.

title: Swap fp16 attention keys for product-quantized codes scored by lookup
idea: Substitute arithmetic on dequantized keys with table lookups. Each cached key becomes 8-16 one-byte product-quantization codes; at decode the query builds a small sub-vector dot-product table, and scores are summed from lookups over the codes, while values use 2-4-bit group quantization. This runs on existing GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Shrinks the KV cache 6-10x and the bytes read per token similarly (fact 5), so the same HBM serves several times more context.

title: Swap fixed-precision KV for age-graded fading precision
idea: Substitute uniform precision with human-like memory decay. KV entries are written at 8 bits; a background kernel requantizes them to 4 bits after ~1k tokens and 2 bits after ~8k, then evicts them, unless their cumulative attention mass marks them salient. This is pure software on unchanged HBM.
why: Long contexts average about 3 bits per element instead of 16, a ~5x KV cut that keeps important tokens sharp.

title: Swap per-request RAG prefill for shared position-independent chunk KV
idea: Substitute per-request KV with a shared library of chunk KV. Each popular retrieval chunk is prefilled once at position zero; at use, its RoPE keys are re-rotated to the real offset and only the first ~5% boundary tokens are recomputed to restore cross-chunk attention, so concurrent requests reference one copy. No memory interface change.
why: RAG serving duplicates the same document KV across users. Sharing it cuts KV footprint 3-10x for popular corpora and saves prefill compute.

title: Swap full KV heads for a shared low-rank latent via SVD retrofit
idea: Substitute full K and V with one latent per token: an existing model's K and V projections are factored jointly by SVD into a rank-r down-projection, the up-projections are absorbed into the query and output matrices, and a brief fine-tune follows (an MLA-style retrofit). This runs on today's GPUs and unchanged HBM.
why: Cuts KV 4-8x for models already deployed, without pretraining from scratch.

title: Swap HBM-resident MoE experts for host-DDR experts with lookahead gating
idea: Substitute 'all experts resident' with 'experts on call'. All experts sit in standard host DDR5 with a hot-expert cache in HBM; a tiny predictor applies the next layer's router to the current hidden state, so the needed experts are DMA'd over existing PCIe/NVLink one layer ahead.
why: MoE models activate ~5-10% of experts per token. HBM holding 20-30% of expert weights cuts HBM per model 3-4x and moves the rest to cheaper DDR bits.

title: Swap fp32 vector-index embeddings for 1-bit codes plus SSD rerank
idea: Substitute full-precision vectors in DRAM with sign-bit codes. Vector databases keep only binary codes in DRAM for Hamming-distance candidate search (popcount on existing CPUs) and read the fp32 vectors of the top ~100 candidates from NVMe to rerank.
why: Billion-vector RAG and search indexes shrink ~25x in DRAM at about a 1-point recall loss, with unchanged DDR.

title: Swap 3x in-memory replication for erasure-coded cache shards
idea: Substitute full replicas with parity. In-memory stores and caches split each object into k data shards plus m parity shards (e.g., 10+4) across nodes and read any k of them in parallel over RDMA. This is pure software on standard servers.
why: Fault-tolerance memory overhead drops from 3.0x to 1.4x, freeing ~50% of the DRAM in replicated cache tiers, and parallel reads cut tail latency.

title: Swap fixed GC heap sizing for cluster memory-price-driven heaps
idea: Substitute DRAM headroom with CPU cycles when DRAM is dear. The scheduler publishes a live per-GB memory price, and the JVM, Go, .NET and V8 runtimes read it to retune their heap targets: they collect more often and return pages when memory is expensive and grow when it is cheap. Unchanged hardware.
why: Managed runtimes keep 1.5-3x the live set as headroom. Price-driven sizing reclaims 20-40% of managed-heap DRAM fleet-wide for a few percent of CPU.

title: Swap live background-tab heaps for pixel-and-state snapshots
idea: Substitute a background tab's DOM and JS heap (often 100-500 MB) with a compressed screenshot plus URL, scroll position and form state. The browser rehydrates the tab by reload and state replay on focus, and service-worker caches make the reload fast. No hardware change.
why: Background tabs dominate client memory, so PCs could ship 8 GB instead of 16 GB for typical users, cutting client DRAM demand.

title: Swap block-compressed game textures for neural latent textures
idea: Substitute BC7 textures (8 bits per texel) with small neural latent grids plus a per-material MLP, decoded by pixel shaders on existing tensor cores at ~1-2 bits per texel in the same GDDR/HBM.
why: Textures are 50-70% of game VRAM. 4-6x compression lets GPUs ship with half the memory at equal fidelity on today's hardware.

title: Swap declared field widths for profile-narrowed fields with overflow escape
idea: Substitute programmer-declared widths with observed widths. A profile-guided compiler pass finds struct fields and arrays whose values fit fewer bits (64-bit ints below 2^16, integral doubles), re-lays them narrow with hot/cold structure splitting, and adds an escape bit that boxes rare outliers into a side table.
why: Data-heavy C/C++/Rust services often waste 30-50% of struct bytes, so heaps shrink 1.3-1.8x on unchanged DDR.

title: Swap generic LZ4 page compression for per-app trained dictionaries
idea: Substitute a one-size codec with app-specific dictionaries. zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per cgroup from sampled pages (repeated object headers, layouts, strings), compresses that app's cold pages with it, and retrains nightly. It is a kernel-only change.
why: Raises cold anonymous-memory compression from ~2.5x to ~4-5x, so the same DIMMs hold 30-50% more working set.

title: Swap greedy tensor allocators for ILP-planned rematerialization and packing
idea: Substitute runtime greedy allocation with a solved plan. One integer program over the training graph decides jointly which activations to keep, recompute or offload and their exact arena offsets, removing fragmentation and peak-coincident lifetimes before the run.
why: Training peak memory falls 2-4x versus caching allocators with heuristic checkpointing, for ~10-20% extra compute, on unchanged HBM.

title: Swap regional peak provisioning for follow-the-sun memory-heavy scheduling
idea: Substitute local peaks with a global flat curve. Memory-hungry, latency-tolerant jobs (batch analytics, embedding builds, offline inference, evals) are checkpointed and moved to regions in their local night, when interactive services leave DRAM idle.
why: Diurnal swings leave 30-40% of DRAM idle at night. Filling those troughs lets fleets buy ~15-25% less DRAM for the same work, with no hardware change.

title: Swap full fine-tuned model copies for 1-bit deltas over one base
idea: Substitute per-customer full checkpoints with sign-bit delta matrices plus one scale per row, applied by a fused GEMM kernel over a single resident base model. Full-rank fine-tunes are covered, not just LoRAs, on existing GPUs.
why: Each 70B variant drops from ~140 GB to ~9 GB, a ~15x memory cut for multi-tenant model hosting.

title: Swap per-parameter Adam moments for count-sketch shared moment tables
idea: Substitute one moment slot per parameter with a hashed count-sketch about 1/10 the size: each parameter maps to several buckets, the median is taken on read, and exact moments are kept only for heavily updated embedding rows. Optimizer code only.
why: Adam state is 2x fp32 per parameter, often larger than the weights themselves. A sketch cuts optimizer HBM/DRAM 5-10x, so a model trains on fewer GPUs' worth of memory.

title: Swap stored embedding rows for IDs hashed through a tiny MLP
idea: Substitute lookup with generation. Recommendation models replace multi-TB ID embedding tables with deep hash embeddings: k hash functions turn each ID into a dense code, a small shared MLP produces the embedding on the fly, and exact rows are kept only for the hottest 1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommendation DRAM, and generating rows cuts them 10-100x at small accuracy cost on unchanged servers.

title: Swap random request placement for document-affinity routing of long contexts
idea: Substitute random load balancing with context-aware routing. The balancer fingerprints each request's large shared context (a codebase, a contract, a transcript) and sends every request on that context to one GPU group, replicating hot documents only when queue depth demands.
why: The same document KV is otherwise duplicated across replicas. Affinity turns N copies into ~1-2, saving 3-10x KV for shared documents, with no hardware change.

title: Swap uncompressed line storage for controller compression with ECC-hidden metadata
idea: Substitute raw line storage with compressed lines whose compression tag hides in unused ECC code-space encodings. The SoC controller compresses each 64 B line (zero, base-delta, frequent-pattern) and packs compressible pages 2:1, with no separate metadata lookups. Standard DDR5 RDIMMs, JEDEC commands and timings stay unchanged, and the OS sees elastic capacity with a balloon for overflow.
why: Server memory typically compresses 1.5-2x. Hiding metadata in ECC removes the metadata-cache penalty that held back earlier schemes, giving 30-60% more effective capacity on existing DIMMs.

title: Swap DRAM-blind procurement for mandatory memory-per-workload efficiency labels
idea: Substitute 'buy more RAM' with buyer pressure on software. Government and large-enterprise procurement require a measured GB-per-active-user or GB-per-transaction label under a standard benchmark (an Energy Star equivalent), give preference points to the top quartile, and require shared runtimes instead of a bundled browser engine per app.
why: Software bloat drives DRAM demand. Pressure on a few large vendors could cut client and server footprints 10-30% within one refresh cycle, with zero hardware change.
